query: Consider the following context: Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates might be expected to reduce scattering times and, therefore, decrease thermal conductivity. In that context, which material can be used for lattice heat conductivity, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys based on elements like tungsten (e.g., a W–Ta–Cr–V alloy), the presence of short‐range order (SRO) precipitates will scatter phonons more effectively than in a fully homogeneous solid solution. This increased phonon scattering reduces phonon lifetimes (i.e. scattering times) and so lowers the lattice contribution to thermal conductivity.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) such as a W–Ta–Cr–V system in a single‐phase solid solution with minimal precipitate formation
generation.intervention: Introduce or promote the formation of SRO precipitates (e.g., through controlled alloying, thermal treatments, or irradiation) within the HEA microstructure
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions and/or irradiation environments where lattice (phonon) conduction is a significant contributor to overall heat transport
generation.structural_mediator: SRO precipitates that act as phonon scattering centers
generation.mechanism: The SRO precipitates create local vibrational inhomogeneities that increase the rate of phonon scattering. This reduces the phonon mean free path and scattering times, thereby decreasing the lattice thermal conductivity relative to a homogeneous alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a higher density of SRO precipitates will show a measurably lower lattice thermal conductivity (i.e., reduced thermal transport via phonons) compared to the baseline HEA without such precipitates
generation.baseline: The refractory HEA in its homogeneous, single‐phase state (with minimal SRO or precipitate formation) where phonon conduction is less impeded
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be most relevant in regimes where the lattice (phonon) contribution dominates heat conduction (e.g., when the electronic contribution is relatively low) and before precipitate coarsening or phase separation alters the microstructure substantially
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the thermal conductivity reduction is uncertain and will depend on the precipitate size, density, and distribution as well as on operating temperature and irradiation dose. Detailed quantitative relationships remain to be determined under practical conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of W–Ta–Cr–V refractory HEA samples in which the SRO precipitate density is systematically varied (e.g., by adjusting thermal treatment or irradiation conditions) while keeping the other parameters constant. Measure the lattice thermal conductivity using methods such as laser flash analysis. Correlate the measured conductivity with microstructural quantification of SRO precipitates (via TEM and/or XRD).
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM, XRD) to quantify precipitate size and density
Lattice thermal conductivity via laser flash or related techniques
If possible, phonon lifetime measurements (e.g., via inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the density or size of the SRO precipitates does not correspond to a statistically significant reduction in the measured lattice thermal conductivity compared to the homogeneous baseline, or if thermal conductivity remains unchanged, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The design stage of the quinary HEA started with the calculation of the thermophysical parameters, mainly enthalpy of mixing (∆ H mix ), entropy of mixing ( Δ S mix ), atomic size difference ( δ ), and the omega parameter ( Ω ) for several compositions. The ability of a material to form a single-phase was empirically shown to depend on these three parameters. For that, the value for Δ H mix was recommended to be in the range of −15 to 5 kJ per mole, while δ should be smaller than 6.6 and Ω larger than 1.1 [26] , [27] . ∆ H mix , δ , and Ω were then calculated using Eqs. 1 – 4 respectively. Other theoretical parameters such as density ( ρ ), melting temperature ( T m ), and VEC were calculated using the rule of mixture, as shown in Eq. 5 , where i represents the element type, X represents the property, r is the atomic radius, and c represents the concentration of element i .

The atomic radii and enthalpy used in the calculations are taken from refs. [28] , [29] , respectively. The base material for this design was the W-Ta-Cr-V HEA which shows high mechanical strength and radiation resistance to loop and He bubble formation under ion irradiation [22] .
